title: The Almost Sale: Where Festive Revenue Slips Away Between Diwali and New Year
summary: Indian D2C brands lose festive sales at checkout through drop-offs, blanket discounts, peak payment failures and COD returns. Here’s how to fix each one.

##


**You were almost there**


Every founder who sells on their own website knows this moment. The ads worked. The shopper landed, liked the product, added it to the cart, and started checking out. You could see it on the dashboard. Then nothing. No order. No message. Just a cart sitting there.


**We call it the almost sale. The customer had already said yes. The sale was lost after that, somewhere between the cart and the money reaching your account.**


Most brands feel this during Diwali week and move on. But the festive season in India does not end with Diwali. It runs all the way to New Year, and every peak in between brings its own version of the same loss. This piece looks at where those sales slip away, why it happens more in the festive months, and what you can fix before your next sale goes live.


##


**The festive season is longer than one week**


Between October and January, a D2C brand goes through not one peak but several:


- **Diwali and Bhai Dooj:** gifting, hampers, home and fashion. The highest intent and the highest traffic of the year.
- **Wedding season (mid-November to February):** ethnic wear, jewellery, beauty and gifting. Bigger orders, and shoppers who think harder before they pay.
- **Black Friday and Cyber Monday:** now a real sale event in India, especially for younger, deal-hunting shoppers.
- **Christmas and year-end sales:** more gifting, plus end-of-season clearance.
- **New Year:** resolution buys in fitness, wellness and self-care.


Each one is a short window with a lot of traffic. That is good news, but it also means every leak in your checkout gets tested five times in ten weeks. A small leak in a normal month becomes a big one when traffic is three times higher. Here are the four we see most often.


##


**Hurdle 1: The shopper who quit at checkout**


Your shopper is not leaving because they changed their mind about the product. They leave because the checkout asked for too much.


Create an account. Wait for the OTP. Type the full address, pincode and landmark. Pick a payment method. All of it on a phone, on a patchy network, while doing three other things. Every extra step is a reason to say “baad mein karta hoon.” And “baad mein” rarely comes back.


In the festive months this gets worse. Shoppers compare across five tabs, buy gifts for several people at once and often shop late at night. The brand with the shortest path to “Paid” usually wins.


**What helps:** a checkout where the shopper enters a mobile number, the OTP fills itself, and the address and preferred payment method are already there from earlier purchases. One page, a few taps, done. Same shopper, same intent, far fewer chances to drop off.


##


**Hurdle 2: The discount that bought orders, not profit**


This one never shows up as a lost sale. It shows up later, in the P&L.


You run a 40% festive offer. Orders go up 3x and the team celebrates. Then the numbers come in, and the margin is thinner than in an ordinary month, sometimes negative.


A simple, illustrative example: a ₹1,000 order with a ₹400 discount, ₹550 product cost and ₹130 in shipping and fees. You lose ₹80 on every order.


The problem is not the discount. It is who got it. The same 40% went to loyal customers who would have paid full price, to one-item carts that barely cover shipping, and to COD orders that may never be delivered.


**What helps:** offers that work at checkout, for the right shopper. A free gift once the cart crosses a set value. An extra discount only for prepaid orders. A relevant add-on just before payment. You still run a festive sale, but every rupee of discount is doing a job.


**How many almost sales did you have last season?** Our team will show you exactly where they slipped away.


**[Check your almost sales](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdWua1tHMoRcxiSjVbmxO1RJxGZ8gMcTbphvAleP3D0fz4sng/viewform)**


##


**Hurdle 3: The payment that failed at the busiest minute**


Your biggest sale goes live at midnight. By 12:05, traffic is at its highest of the year. This is exactly when a bank’s servers slow down, a UPI app times out or the checkout page takes a few seconds too long to load.


The shopper tries once, maybe twice. Then they close the tab, and they may not come back for the rest of the sale. You paid for that traffic through ads, influencers and emails, and lost it at the very last step.


Peak-hour failures are hard to spot from the outside. Your dashboard shows a dip in conversion, not “one bank was down for 11 minutes.” By the time you notice, the peak is over.


**What helps:** a checkout and payment setup built for festive load, one that sends a payment through another route when a bank is slow, and a team you can actually reach at 2 am on sale night. Test it before the sale, not during.


##


**Hurdle 4: The COD order that came back**


COD is still how a large share of Indian shoppers prefer to buy, especially in smaller cities and on a first order with a new brand. It gets you the sale. It does not guarantee the money.


You pack the order, pay to ship it, and at the door the customer says no. Maybe they found it cheaper elsewhere, maybe they changed their mind, maybe they were never serious. Saying yes to COD cost them nothing. Saying no costs you shipping both ways, packaging, and stock stuck in transit during your best selling weeks.


In wedding season and at year-end, when order values go up, each return hurts more.


**What helps:** three things at checkout, before the order ships. Flag high-risk COD orders using pincode and buyer history. Ask for a small token amount upfront, say ₹99, with the rest on delivery. And give shoppers a real reason to pay online, like an extra discount on prepaid. A shopper who has already paid something is far more likely to accept the parcel.


##


**Fix it before the next peak, not after**


None of these leaks are new. What changes in the festive months is how often you hit them, and how much traffic you have already paid for when you do.


Before your next sale, ask yourself four questions:


1. How many steps does a new shopper take from cart to “Paid”? Try it on your own phone, on mobile data.
2. Who got your last discount, and how much of it went to customers who would have bought anyway?
3. What was your payment success rate in the busiest hour of your last sale?
4. What share of your COD orders came back, and what did each return cost you?


If any answer makes you wince, that is where your almost sales are.

There are still five sale moments left before New Year. Make sure “bas ho hi gaya tha” is not how this season ends.
